27. Now let us take up r he second contention of the learned Advocate, that b, with regard to malafide exercise of power by the executive. It has been stated in the application that the detenu was arrested from their Khulna Residence by the Rakkhi Bahini on May 26, 1974 and was forwarded straight to the Khulna District Jail without producing him before any Court of law. On the next day an order under Section 3 (2) of the Special Powers Act, 1974 was served upon him stating that his detention becomes necessary to prevent him from doing any act which is likely to prejudice the security of Bangladesh and maintenance of Public Order. According to the petitioner the arrest was wholly illegal and without any authority, which cannot be validated by a supplementary order of detention passed under the Special Powers Act. It has been further stated that the detenu was never involved in politics during his student life nor he delivered any speech anywhere in Bangladesh and the alleged charges brought against him are false Malicious and out of grudge. According to the petitioner the grounds for detention are not relatable to the purposes of detention but the same were drawn lip without any foundation. In the counter affidavit in opposition it has been stated that it is not correct to say that the detenu has been detained illegally and with malafide intention to feed fat someones political grudge; but the correct position is that the detenu has been detained lawfully in view of his past activities and also to prevent him from committing prejudicial acts likely to endanger public life, and create law and order situation and overthrow by violent means the government established by law. It has been further stated that the detenu took active part in politics in his student life; he was elected General Secretary, Khulna City Chhatra League in 1970; he was elected as the General Secretary in Sundarban College Chhatra Sangshad in the same year; in March 1971 he was elected General Secretary, Swadhin Bangladesh Chhatra Sangram Parisad , Khulna District Unit; in 1972 he was elected as one of the members of the Canvassing Committee of J.S.D. Khulna; and in earl v 1973 he was elected as the publicity Secretary of J.S. D. Khulna. The facts stated in the affidavit in opposition have not been controverted in the affidavit in reply filed by the petitioner. Therefore this goes unchallenged that the detenu took active part in the student politics in the years 1970,1971 and 1972, and in the early part of 1973. The detenu was associated with the City Chhatra League, the Sundarban College Chhatra Sangshad SwadhinBangladesh Chhatra Sangram Parisad. Participation in the student politics as alleged against the detenu, cannot by itself justify an order of detention. In the affidavit in opposition of thing has been stated as to whether the organisation mentioned therein, indulged in activities which endangered law and order situation and public safety. In the affidavit in opposition it has been only stated that the petitioner was arrested for detention on May 26, 1974. The Additional District Magistrate, Khulna who passed the detention order, reported the matter to the Government with the grounds of detention, and the Government approved the detention and passed the order on June 24,1974 detaining the detenu under section 3 (1) or the Special Powers Act. From the above statement it is clear that the order of detention passed under sub-section (1) of section 3 by the Government of Bangladesh was made merely on the basis of the communication received from the Additional District Magistrate, Khulna. Apart from the grounds served upon the detenu on May 27, 1974, there were no other materials before the authority who passed the detention order under section 3 (1). The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner rightly submitted that the order of detention had been made not for the purpose of meeting any requirement of the Special Powers Act, but for a collateral purpose of creating a situation not congenial for the purpose of growing of an effective political opposition. From the affidavits of the parties we find there is sufficient scope for making a grievance that the detention order was made for a collateral purpose of stifling growth of an effective political opposition. Legitimate criticism of the policy pursued by the rulling party had nothing to do with the Public order. In a case where 'mala fide' is alleged it does not mean that improper motive is attributed to the detaining authority. A detention order is made mala fide when there is malice in law although there is no malice in Tact; and the malice in law is to be inferred when an order is made contrary to the object and purposes of the Act or when the detaining authority permits himself to be influenced by conditions which he ought not to permit. This was the observation made by Chagla C.J. of the Bombay High Court in the case of Maledath Bhratham Malyali Vs. the Commissioner of Police, A.I.R. 1950 Bom. 202 (F.B.) after making the above observation the learned Chief Justice held;- 

 30. It hardly needs any discussion to corn to the conclusion that even this ground suffers from vagueness. Membership of a political organisation, not declared unlawful, by it cannot be a ground for detention. As the nature of the prejudicial activities of the political organisation concerned, and the activities of the detenu in the District of Khulna, nothing has been disclosed in the ground. The alleged activities of the detenu appear to be of the year 1972 and 1973 and early part of 1974. The learned Deputy Attorney General admitted that all the activities mentioned are the past activities of the detenu that is therefore the Special Powers Act, 1974 came into being. When the, grounds of detention suffer from vagueness, it has been consistently held by the Superior Courts of the Sub-Continent that the order of detention passed on such grounds cannot be sustained. This principle of law, practically has grown en the well-thought observation made by, Kania C.J. of the Supreme Court of India, in the case of the State of Bombay Vs. Atma Ram Sridhar Yaidya, A.I.R. 1951 (S. C.) 157. Petitioner At ma Ram was, arrested under the Preventive Detention Act 1950 and grounds for his detention were surfed upon him. They were in the following term: "That you are engaged and are likely to be engaged in promoting acts of sabotage on railway and railway property, in Greater Bombay". In the habeas corpus petition the petitioner contained that the sole aim of the Government in ordering his detention was not the preservation of public order or the security of the State, but the locking of active trade unionists that belonged to the All India Trade Union Congress. He contended that the grounds is "delightfully vague and does not mention when, where or what kind of sabotage or how the applicant promoted it." "He further urged that the ground gave no particulars and, therefore, was net a ground as required to be furnished under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950. The Petitioner asserted that the detaining authority acted malafide, for a collateral purpose, outside the scope of the Act, and that the applicant's detention in any event" as illegal and malafide.
